variants.title: Thermal conductivity at low T: 304 stainless steel
variants.sample: 304 stainless steel rod, a disordered alloy (SIMULATED)
variants.method: steady-state heat flow from 1 to 20 K
variants.unknown: thermal conductivity against T, kappa at 4.2 K
variants.note: An alloy conducts poorly and almost linearly in T (no phonon peak, no Wiedemann-Franz electrons dominating): that is why cryostat supports are stainless. The power law kappa = 0.06 T^1.1 W/(m K) is an order-of-magnitude stand-in for the NIST curve, from memory - verify.

source.title: NIST cryogenic material properties: 304 stainless steel

variants.title: Thermal conductivity at low T: a sapphire crystal (phonon peak)
variants.sample: Sapphire (Al2O3) single-crystal rod, 1 mm boundary length (SIMULATED)
variants.method: steady-state heat flow from 1 to 60 K
variants.unknown: thermal conductivity against T, the phonon peak, the boundary mean free path
variants.note: At the lowest temperatures phonons cross the crystal without scattering, so kappa = (2 pi^2 kB^4 ell/(15 hbar^3 v^2)) T^3 (Casimir) and kappa/T^3 gives the boundary length ell; higher up Umklapp scattering cuts it off, so kappa peaks. The sound velocity, Debye temperature and Umklapp strength are illustrative, from memory - verify.

source.title: R. Berman, Thermal Conduction in Solids (Oxford, 1976): Casimir boundary scattering
